title: The man on the road
hook: Upaka the wanderer hears him, shakes his head, and takes another road (MN 26)

segments.voice: Yesterday, should he teach? Brahma pleaded, and the Buddha saw people like lotuses at every depth. Your line was some are ready. Who did you share something with? Day sixty.

You've found something that changed your life. A book, a practice, a way of seeing. You're bursting to share it. And the very first person you tell looks at you politely, says, huh, good for you, and changes the subject. It stings. Maybe you even wonder if you got it wrong. The Buddha has decided to teach. He's thought about who should hear first, and he's chosen his five old companions, the ones who left him when he ate. They're in a deer park near Varanasi, a long walk away. So he sets out on the road. And not far along it, he meets a stranger. Today, the man on the road.
screen: `HUH, GOOD FOR YOU.` → `A LONG WALK TO THE FIVE.` → `A STRANGER ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: The stranger's name is Upaka. He's a wanderer too, from a group called the Ajivikas, and he's struck by what he sees. Your face is so clear, friend, he says. Your skin so bright. Who's your teacher? Whose teaching do you follow? It's the perfect opening. The very first question anyone asks the Buddha about his teaching. And the Buddha answers, the sutta says, in verse. He says he has no teacher; he found this himself. He has overcome everything, understood everything, and he's on his way to Kasi to set the wheel of the teaching turning, to beat the drum of the deathless in a world gone blind. It's a big answer. Upaka listens. And then he says something like: may it be so, friend. He shakes his head. And he takes a side road, and walks away. That's it. The first person the Buddha ever tells about his awakening doesn't buy it. The Buddha himself tells this story, and doesn't hide it. He doesn't chase Upaka. He doesn't argue. He just keeps walking to the deer park. There's a coda, from the later tradition. Years afterward, the story goes, Upaka fell in love and married a hunter's daughter named Capa, had a son, and later, unhappy, went looking for the Buddha after all, and became a monk. Capa's own verses survive in the Therigatha, the poems of the early nuns. So the man on the road wasn't lost. He just wasn't ready yet.
screen: `WHO'S YOUR TEACHER?` · `NO TEACHER. I FOUND IT.` · `MAY IT BE SO. A SIDE ROAD.` · `NOT LOST. JUST NOT YET.` · then, large: `NOT EVERYONE IS READY.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Think of someone who disagrees with you about something that matters to you. It might be small, a movie, or big, how to live. Picture them shaking their head and walking off down a side road. Notice what rises in you: the urge to chase, to argue, to prove. Let it be there. Then, gently, let them go. You can wish them well on their road. You keep walking yours. The bell holds the time.
The man on the road. Upaka, the first person the Buddha ever told, who said may it be so, shook his head, and took another road.
screen: `THE MAN ON THE ROAD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: not everyone is ready. Today, let someone disagree with you, and don't chase them down the side road. Day sixty.

howItsDone: Buddhists retell Upaka's meeting as a reminder not to force the teaching on anyone, and Buddhist teachers traditionally teach only when asked, letting people come and go freely.

fork.setup: you're Upaka. a wanderer with a shining face tells you he's found the deathless with no teacher at all. what do you do?
options: say may it be so, shake your head, and take a side road.
fork.reveal: Upaka takes the side road. the first person to hear doesn't believe. and the Buddha doesn't chase him.

original.note: Pali: an Ajivika, a member of the wandering group Upaka belonged to.

trapdoor: what you thought: everyone who met the Buddha was converted on the spot.
what it means: the very first person he told shook his head and walked away, and the Buddha let him go.
what a scholar hears: MN 26 records Upaka the Ajivika's 'may it be so, friend' (hupeyya), his head-shake and the bypath; the commentary and Therigatha (Capa's verses) tell of his later return.

sources.ref: Ariyapariyesana Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 26): the meeting with Upaka

notes: MN 26 paraphrased: Upaka's question, the Buddha's verses (no teacher, the drum of the deathless at Kasi/Benares), 'may it be so, friend', head-shake, bypath. Confirm.
The coda (Upaka marries Capa, has a son, later ordains) is from the commentary and the Therigatha verses of Capa. Confirm details and whether to keep.
'Kasi' is the region with Varanasi (Benares); the hook says 'near Varanasi'. Confirm.
